---
title: Dfsu
---


Dfsu and mesh files are both flexible mesh file formats used by MIKE 21/3 engines. 
The .mesh file is an ASCII file for storing the flexible mesh geometry. 
The .dfsu file is a binary dfs file with data on this mesh. The mesh geometry is 
available in a .dfsu file as static items.  


For a detailed description of the .mesh and .dfsu file specification see the [flexible file format documentation](../FM_FileSpecification.pdf).


## The flexible mesh

The mesh geometry in a .mesh or a .dfsu file consists of a list of nodes and a list of elements.

Each node has:

* Node id
* x,y,z coordinates
* Code (0 for internal water points, 1 for land, >1 for open boundary)

Each element has:

* Element id
* Element table; specifies for each element the nodes that defines the element. 
(the number of nodes defines the type: triangular, quadrilateral, prism etc.)


::: callout-note
In MIKE Zero, node ids, element ids and layer ids are 1-based.  In MIKE IO, all ids are **0-based** following standard Python indexing. That means, as an example, that when finding the element closest to a point its id will be 1 lower in MIKE IO compared to examining the file in MIKE Zero.
:::

## MIKE IO Flexible Mesh Geometry 

MIKE IO has Flexible Mesh Geometry classes, e.g. [`GeometryFM2D`](`mikeio.spatial.GeometryFM2D`), containing the list of node coordinates and the element table which defines the mesh, as well as a number of derived properties (e.g. element coordinates) and methods making it convenient to work with the mesh. 

If a .dfsu file is *read* with [](`mikeio.read`), the returned Dataset ds will contain a Flexible Mesh Geometry `geometry`. If a .dfsu or a .mesh file is *opened* with [](`mikeio.open`), the returned object will also contain a Flexible Mesh Geometry `geometry`. 

```{python}
import mikeio

ds = mikeio.read("../data/oresundHD_run1.dfsu")
ds.geometry
```

```{python}
dfs = mikeio.open("../data/oresundHD_run1.dfsu")
dfs.geometry
```


## Common Dfsu and Mesh properties

MIKE IO has Dfsu classes for .dfsu files 
and a [Mesh class](`mikeio.Mesh`) for .mesh files which both 
have a [](`mikeio.spatial.GeometryFM2D`)/[](`mikeio.spatial.GeometryFM3D`) accessible through the ´geometry´ accessor. 


## Dfsu types

The following dfsu file types are supported by MIKE IO.

* 2D horizontal. 
* 3D layered. 
* 2D vertical profile - a vertical slice through a 3D layered file. 
* 1D vertical column - a vertical dfs1 file and is produced by taking out one column of a 3D layered file.
* 3D/4D SW, two horizontal dimensions and 1-2 spectral dimensions. Output from MIKE 21 SW.

When a dfsu file is opened with mikeio.open() the returned dfs object will be a specialized class [Dfsu2DH](`mikeio.dfsu.Dfsu2DH`), [Dfsu3D](`mikeio.dfsu.Dfsu3D`), [Dfsu2DV](`mikeio.dfsu.Dfsu2DV`), or [DfsuSpectral](`mikeio.dfsu.DfsuSpectral`) according to the type of dfsu file. 

The layered files (3d, 2d/1d vertical) can have both sigma- and z-layers or only sigma-layers.


In most cases values are stored in cell centers and vertical (z) information in nodes, 
but the following values types exists: 

* Standard value type, storing values on elements and/or nodes. This is the default type.
* Face value type, storing values on element faces. This is used e.g. for HD decoupling files, to store the discharge between elements.
* Spectral value type, for each node or element, storing vales for a number of frequencies and/or directions. This is the file type for spectral output from the MIKE 21 SW. 


## Visualization

### Geometry

The geometry (bathymetry) can be visualized in various ways.

```{python}
geom  = dfs.geometry
geom.plot();
```

```{python}
geom.plot.mesh();
```

```{python}
geom.plot(vmin=-20);
```


```{python}
geom.plot.contour(levels=[-20,-10], cmap='tab10');
```

```{python}
geom.plot.contourf(levels=6, vmin=-30);
```

### Data

The data can be visualized in a similar way.

```{python}
da = ds["Surface elevation"]
da.plot(cmap='plasma');
```

```{python}
ax = da.plot.contour(show_mesh=True, cmap="tab20")
ax.set_ylim(6135000, 6160000);
```

### Subplots

Pass a matplotlib axes to create side-by-side comparisons:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(ncols=2, figsize=(12, 7))

ds["Surface elevation"].isel(time=-1).plot.contourf(ax=ax1, title="Surface elevation")
ds["V velocity"].isel(time=-1).plot.contourf(
    ax=ax2, title="V velocity", label="Northward velocity [m/s]"
);
```

## Working with data

### Subsetting by element properties

Elements can be selected based on their coordinates, e.g. by depth:

```{python}
import numpy as np

ze = dfs.geometry.element_coordinates[:, 2]
deep_elems = np.where(ze < -20)[0]

ds_deep = dfs.read(items=0, time=-1, elements=deep_elems)
ax = ds_deep[0].plot()
dfs.geometry.plot.mesh(ax=ax);
```

### Boolean masking

Instead of reading a subset, you can mask values directly on a DataArray:

```{python}
da_last = ds["Surface elevation"].isel(time=-1).copy()
da_last[ze >= -20] = np.nan
da_last.plot(show_mesh=True);
```

## 3D layered files: z-coordinates

Layered 3D dfsu files (and the vertical-profile / vertical-column slices derived
from them) carry a time-varying vertical coordinate at every mesh node. MIKE IO
exposes this through the `.z` accessor on a `DataArray` (or `Dataset`):

```{python}
ds3d = mikeio.read("../data/oresund_sigma_z.dfsu")
da3d = ds3d["Temperature"]
da3d.z.nodes.shape       # (n_time, n_nodes) — z at every mesh node, every timestep
```

```{python}
da3d.z.elements.shape    # (n_time, n_elements) — mean of each element's node z's
```

`da.z.nodes` returns the raw node z-coordinates exactly as stored in the file;
`da.z.elements` is derived as the per-element mean of the column-node z's and is
cached on first access. The same accessor is available on Datasets
(`ds.z.nodes`, `ds.z.elements`) and is delegated to the first item.

### Total amount of a substance

`volume_integral()` sums concentration times element volume over the model
domain, one value per timestep. The element volumes follow the moving free
surface. The example file holds inorganic nitrogen from a MIKE 3 ECO Lab model
of the Odense Estuary at two dates:

```{python}
ds_wq = mikeio.read("../data/odense_rough_3d_wq.dfsu")
nitrogen = ds_wq["IN, Inorganic nitrogen, g N/m3"]
total = nitrogen.volume_integral()
total
```

Inorganic nitrogen is in mg/l, which is g/m³, so the result is the nitrogen mass
in g. Concentrations in µg/l, mg/m³, µg/m³, g/l and kg/m³ give a mass too; for
other units the result has the type "Undefined" and the unit of the values
times m³.

```{python}
total.to_dataframe() / 1e6   # tonnes
```

For part of the domain, select it first:

```{python}
bbox = (212000, 6155000, 217000, 6160000)
nitrogen.sel(area=bbox).volume_integral().to_dataframe()
```

```{python}
polygon = [(212000, 6155000), (217000, 6155000), (217000, 6160000)]
nitrogen.sel(area=polygon).volume_integral().to_dataframe()
```

```{python}
nitrogen.sel(time="2002-01-15").volume_integral()
```

Selecting a single layer returns 2D data without element volumes, so pass the
layers to `volume_integral` instead:

```{python}
nitrogen.volume_integral(layers="top").to_dataframe()
```

```{python}
nitrogen.volume_integral(layers=[0, 1, 2]).to_dataframe()   # the three bottom layers
```

On a Dataset, `volume_integral()` returns the total of every item.

### Volume-weighted mean

```{python}
nitrogen.average(axis="space", weights=nitrogen.z.volume).to_dataframe()
```

`average` checks that a DataArray of weights has the same time and geometry as
the data, so a volume from another selection raises instead of giving a wrong
mean.

A vertical column keeps its z-coordinates, so its thickness can be used as
weights for a depth-averaged value:

```{python}
column = nitrogen.sel(x=221040, y=6163422)
column.average(axis="space", weights=column.z.thickness).to_dataframe()
```

### Layer thickness and element volume

`da.z.thickness` and `da.z.volume` return the per-timestep element thickness and
volume as DataArrays with the same time and geometry as `da`:

```{python}
vol = nitrogen.z.volume
vol
```

The volume is the horizontal element area times the thickness (mean z of the
element's top nodes minus mean z of its bottom nodes). For the horizontal area
alone, use `geometry.element_areas`. The volume can be written to a dfsu file,
e.g. to inspect it in MIKE Zero:

```python
vol.to_dfs("volume.dfsu")
```

### Non-layered DataArrays

For any DataArray whose geometry is not layered (dfs2, 2D dfsu, spectral, …),
accessing `.z` returns a placeholder that raises `AttributeError` to make the
geometry constraint discoverable:

```{python}
#| error: true
ds2 = mikeio.read("../data/random.dfs2")
ds2[0].z.nodes
```

## Creating a dfsu from a mesh

```{python}
import pandas as pd

msh = mikeio.open("../data/odense_rough.mesh")
data = 36.5 * np.ones(msh.geometry.n_elements)
time = pd.date_range("2020-1-1", periods=1)
item = mikeio.ItemInfo(mikeio.EUMType.Chezy_No)

da = mikeio.DataArray(data, time=time, item=item, geometry=msh.geometry)
da.to_dfs("chezy_map.dfsu")
```

```{python}
import os
os.remove("chezy_map.dfsu")
```
